sections.title: Overview
sections.body: Before implementing multi-agent systems, understand the fundamental orchestration patterns.

steps.label: Orchestrator
steps.narration: A coordinator decomposes work and assigns ownership to specialists.

steps.label: Delegate
steps.narration: Tasks are handed off with clear inputs, outputs, and termination conditions.

steps.label: Specialists
steps.narration: Specialist agents execute narrow skills and return structured results.

steps.label: Merge
steps.narration: Results are reconciled; conflicts and duplicates are resolved before final output.

steps.label: Terminate
steps.narration: The workflow must always end — via success, safe failure, timeout, or human decision.

sections.title: 9.1 Prompt chaining — Sequential workflow
sections.body:
Each step receives the output of the previous step.

Example: Resume processing workflow

This is a good architecture when execution steps are known in advance.

For resume parsing, you might not need four autonomous agents. Four well-defined functions or workflow nodes may be easier to test, cheaper and more reliable.

diagram.title: Visual flow — 9.1 Prompt chaining — Sequential workflow

steps.label: Goal
steps.narration: The agent receives a user goal and must decide what information or tools are required.

steps.label: Reason
steps.narration: The model plans the next action instead of answering blindly.

steps.label: Act / tool
steps.narration: The agent calls an authorized tool or function with structured arguments.

steps.label: Observe
steps.narration: Usage, cost, latency, and traces are recorded for FinOps and incident response.

steps.label: Decide
steps.narration: The loop continues, escalates to a human, or finishes with a grounded answer.

sections.title: 9.2 Routing pattern
sections.body:
A classifier determines which specialist workflow should process a request.

Incoming support request

Intent router

Production routing should support an unknown-intent category, multi-intent questions, calibrated classification and escalation when uncertainty is high.

Parallelization reduces latency only when dependencies permit it. It can also increase instantaneous provider quota demand and tail-latency risk.

sections.title: 9.4 Orchestrator-worker pattern
sections.body:
Unlike a fixed parallel workflow, an orchestrator dynamically identifies the subtasks that are necessary.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Complex user goal] --> B[Orchestrator]
    B --> C[Determine required subtasks]
    C --> D[Research worker]
    C --> E[Data analysis worker]
    C --> F[Document review worker]
    D --> G[Aggregate results]
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H[Validate objective completion]
```

For example, a market research agent may determine that some companies require financial analysis while others only require product comparison.

The number of workers must be bounded. Otherwise, an orchestrator can create an unexpectedly expensive fan-out.

sections.title: 9.5 Choosing the right design pattern
sections.body:
| Pattern | Use when | Main risk |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Sequential | Steps and dependencies are known | Unnecessary serial latency |
| Routing | Tasks belong to different domains | Incorrect classification |
| Parallel | Tasks are independent | Fan-out and quota pressure |
| Orchestrator-worker | Subtasks are dynamically discovered | Uncontrolled delegation |
| Evaluator-optimizer | Quality criteria can be tested | Endless refinement |
| Autonomous loop | Next action depends on observations | Unpredictable execution |
| Human-in-the-loop | Important actions require supervision | Approval bottleneck |

Start with the simplest architecture and increase complexity only after measuring its benefit.
